데이터셋에 반응 시간, 평가자 신원, 나이와 같은 공변량 등 추가 정보가 포함된 경우, 해당 정보는 일관된 이름 규칙을 따르는 추가 열에 저장됩니다. 이 하나의 단순한 구조는 매우 다양한 측정 상황을 포괄하며, 이 덕분에 분석 코드를 한 번만 작성하여 저장소 전체에 적용할 수 있습니다.
이 표준에 대한 전체 기술 명세는 itemresponsewarehouse.org/standard.html에서 확인할 수 있습니다. 문항 텍스트, 쌍대 비교(경쟁) 데이터, 명목형(순서 없는 범주) 반응을 위한 보다 전문화된 표준도 별도로 존재합니다.

title: Item Response Warehouse (IRW; 문항 반응 데이터 저장소)
text:
자동화를 얼마나 원하는지에 따라 IRW 데이터를 얻는 세 가지 방법이 있습니다.
1. 웹 브라우저에서 탐색하기 IRW 데이터 브라우저에서 계정 없이도 데이터셋과 그 메타데이터를 바로 탐색할 수 있습니다. 전체 데이터셋을 다운로드하려면 무료 Redivis 계정이 필요합니다. 이는 Redivis가 실제 데이터를 호스팅하는 플랫폼이기 때문입니다.
2. irw 패키지 사용하기 (권장) R과 Python 양쪽에서 모두 사용 가능한 irw 패키지는 데이터를 찾고, 필터링하고, 다운로드하는 간단한 함수들을 제공합니다.
# R
devtools::install_github("itemresponsewarehouse/Rpkg")
library(irw)

irw_info()                     # overview of the IRW
irw_list_tables()              # list all available tables
irw_filter(var = "rt")         # find tables that include response times
df <- irw_fetch("4thgrade_math_sirt")   # download one table
# Python
# pip install "git+https://github.com/itemresponsewarehouse/Python-pkg.git"
import irw

irw.info()
irw.list_tables()
irw.filter(var="rt")
df = irw.fetch("4thgrade_math_sirt")
패키지를 처음 사용할 때는 무료 Redivis 계정으로 로그인하라는 안내를 받게 됩니다. 이후에는 코드 한 줄이면 어떤 데이터셋이든 R이나 Python으로 직접 다운로드할 수 있습니다. 그러면 데이터는 표준 소프트웨어—예를 들어 문항 반응 이론이나 요인분석 패키지—로 바로 분석할 준비가 됩니다.
3. Redivis 클라이언트 라이브러리 직접 사용하기 더 낮은 수준의 작업 흐름이나 R/Python을 사용하지 않는 경우, Redivis 자체의 R 및 Python 클라이언트 라이브러리를 통해서도 데이터에 접근할 수 있습니다. 자세한 내용은 시작하기 가이드를 참고하세요.


IRW 프로젝트에는 다음도 포함됩니다:

점점 늘어나는 비네트(vignettes) 모음 — 여러 IRW 데이터셋에 걸쳐 고전적 및 새로운 측정 방법을 동시에 적용해 보는 실습 예제
실제 데이터를 활용해 심리측정학을 가르치기 위한 교육 자료 및 연습 문제
자신의 데이터셋을 저장소에 추가하고자 하는 연구자를 위한 기여 절차

title: Item Response Warehouse (IRW; 문항 반응 데이터 저장소)
text:
Domingue et al. (2025). An introduction to the Item Response Warehouse (IRW): A resource for enhancing data usage in psychometrics. Behavior Research Methods. doi:10.3758/s13428-025-02796-y
Nadela, Lee, Jain, Gupta, Zhang & Domingue (2026). The Item Response Warehouse: What It Is, How to Use It, and Targets for Potential Improvements. Chinese/English Journal of Educational Measurement and Evaluation. doi:10.59863/CIJG4549
Wilkinson et al. (2016). The FAIR Guiding Principles for scientific data management and stewardship. Scientific Data. doi:10.1038/sdata.2016.18
웹사이트: itemresponsewarehouse.org
코드: github.com/itemresponsewarehouse

연구에 IRW 데이터를 사용하신다면, 원본 데이터를 인용해 주시기 바랍니다(이를 위한 기능을 제공하고 있습니다). 위의 소개 논문도 함께 인용해 주시면 매우 감사하겠습니다.

질문이나 의견이 있으신가요? 데이터셋 기여를 원하시나요? 문의 페이지를 방문하거나 GitHub에 이슈를 등록해 주세요.

title: Item Text
text:
ImportantAbout these data



IRW item text is reconstructed from published articles, codebooks, and supplementary materials using a largely automated pipeline with partial human review. It is provided for research purposes only. We make no guarantee that the text is accurate, complete, or correctly aligned with the item identifiers in the corresponding IRW response data; the original source document is always authoritative. Users are responsible for verifying item text against that source before drawing substantive conclusions. See Known Issues for documented discrepancies, and please get in touch if you find others.
Note also that the licenses recorded for IRW response data do not extend to the instruments themselves. Inclusion of item text here implies no license to reuse an instrument; copyright and related rights remain with the original rights holders, and users are responsible for obtaining any permissions their intended use requires.

title: Item Text
text:
Known issues
The below are known issues affecting the match between item text and the IRW tables.








Warningsingh_2025_identity_pba





Table has 6 items for affiliation but the codebook only has 5 items











Warningpaampsmartsud_saba_2023_ders





The paper described only 36-item, but the IRW table contains 37











Warningnamprb_siwiak_2024_ssub





IRW table doesn’t match the number of items provided in the paper











Warningsv-maia2_randelovic_2021_erq





IRW table uses a 1-5 scale (the paper’s ERQ is normally 1-7); the itemtext anchor labels for the 1-5 version are inferred from the 1-7 wording, not sourced from the study’s own materials











Warningfivpei_perrig_2023_attdiff





Paper has 28 items, IRW contains only 21











Warningoxfordcovid_xue_2024_at





IRW missing the item: media_tv











Warningsocialstereotype_hughes_2025_judgement





IRW has 6 items for affiliation but the codebook only has 5 items











Warninggilbert_meta_51





ch_anemic is not an item in the code book











Warninggilbert_meta_35





item text covers 8 of the 12 values_* items. The other four (values_b, values_h, values_k, values_l) are omitted: the study’s replication do-file builds its democratic-values scale from only eight of the twelve, and no wording is published for the other four. The eight are mapped to their text using the source .dta’s variable labels, which name six of them outright; note that values_e and values_j are reverse-worded, so their response options run in the opposite direction to the other six











Warninggilbert_meta_42





item text covers only 12 of the 20 items – the 4 life_satisfaction_* and 4 locus_of_control_* items are omitted because no item text is available for them. The paper names the source instruments (a 4-item subset of Diener’s Satisfaction With Life Scale, and 4 items from the Levenson Multidimensional Internal Locus of Control Scales, both adapted for the study context) but neither it nor its appendix gives which items were used or their adapted wording, and the openICPSR questionnaire is access-gated











Warninggilbert_meta_38





survey does not contain bought_ins











Warningflorida_twins_friends





Items friends20/friends21 are not documented in the Florida Twin Project’s Wave 1 Child Survey Measures codebook; the other 19 items match exactly











Warningaddy_2021_sdq_ghana





SDQ_7’s response options run in reverse order in the source codebook (0=certainly true … 2=not true) relative to the other 9 items; transcribed as given, so this item may need reverse-coding











Warningaguirre_camacho_2021_shai





Item text is the English SHAI-18 original, but the study administered a Spanish translation whose wording the paper never quotes. The instrument has no item stems – each item is a group of four statements – so all text sits in option_text and item_text is empty. The 14/4 split between the two subscales is confirmed against the paper’s subscale statistics, but item order within each subscale rests on HAnx<N> being the instrument’s item N











Warningaguirre_camacho_2021_champion





Item text is the administered Spanish wording, but the 1/5 scale anchors are recorded in English because the source labels only the endpoints and only in English; the middle three points are unlabeled











Warningabdullah_2024_bsq_sevgen





The source papers state per-item scale ranges that do not match the data: items 3/4/6 are documented 1-5 but only reach 4, and item 7 is documented 1-7 but shows 1-4 plus 6-7. SEVG2 is published in the instrument but absent from the table











Warningajaykumar_2023_nasa_tlx





Item text is the official NASA-TLX rating-scale definitions, not the study’s own wording: the study administered a modified NASA-TLX on a 5-point scale and never published what participants saw, so the exact phrasing differs. The paper’s own analyses use three of these six items











Warningalexander_2017_dsi





Covers only the Differentiation of Self Inventory’s Emotional Reactivity and Emotional Cutoff subscales (23 of the 43 items). The dsi_1..dsi_23 to original-item mapping is reconstructed from the published appendix order rather than documented in the source, though it matches both the published subscale key and the response data











Warningalgner2022_cse





Item text is the English CSES original; the study administered a German translation whose exact wording could not be located











Warningalcoholhealthwarninglabel_brennan_2022_awareness_harms_followup





resp (0/1) is a derived binary rather than the original response scale: the study collapsed a 7-point agree/disagree item into aware/not-aware, so option_text records that rule rather than a literal option label











Warningdumas_organisciak_2022





Paper describes originality coded on a 0-4 scale; the IRW table is on 1-5. Whether this is an intentional shift during processing or an unverified discrepancy is unresolved











Warning16_personalityfactors





The source’s own instructions describe the scale as “(1) disagree … (5) agree” while its per-item codebook labels it “strongly disagree … strongly agree”; option_text follows the codebook. Item 163 is the one column the codebook omits, so its text comes from the IPIP scale listing rather than the dataset’s own documentation











Warningalgner2022_uwes





Both the UWES-9 instrument and this paper describe the response scale as 0-6 (Nie … Immer), but the study’s own data records the same seven categories as 1-7, so a response of 1 here corresponds to the instrument’s 0 (Nie). Item text is Schaufeli & Bakker’s official German UWES-9, while the paper cites a different German version (Sautier et al. 2015) whose wording was not obtainable











Warningalmuqbil_2022_epds





Participants completed the Arabic EPDS translation (Ghubash et al. 1997); the item text here is the English wording used to label the items in the study’s own data file, so it is not what respondents read











Warningalkouri_2025_icu_stressors





The source questionnaire changes the wording of its second response option partway through the scale – items 01-14 offer “Barely” and items 15-29 offer “Rarely” for the same value 2 – so option text varies by item; transcribed as the source gives it











Warningalsuhibani_2022_loc





The paper’s Methods describes this as a five-point scale, but the live data and the study’s own SPSS file both show a genuine 6-point “Strongly disagree” … “Strongly agree” scale; the data file was followed rather than the paper text











Warningalves_2017_hamd17





Item text follows a canonical reproduction of Hamilton’s original (1960) HDRS-17, which scores item 9 (Agitation) 0-2, but this study’s data scores it 0-4 – so HamD9Baixa responses of 3 and 4 have no option label. Item text is also a canonical reproduction rather than the study’s own materials, and item-to-text alignment follows the instrument’s standard order rather than an explicit map











Warningaltahla_2024_whoqol





Participants were Chinese adults who completed a Chinese-language version; the item text here is the English wording used to label the items in the study’s own data file, so it is not what respondents read











Warningaltahla_2024_whoqol_bref





Participants were Chinese adults who completed a Chinese-language version; the item text here is the English wording used to label the items in the study’s own data file, so it is not what respondents read. This table is also the spinal-cord-injury subsample of altahla_2024_whoqol, whose responses it duplicates











Warningaltahla_2024_swls





Participants were Chinese adults who completed a Chinese-language version; the item text here is the English wording used to label the items in the study’s own data file, so it is not what respondents read











Warningamarilla_2020_lawton_brody





resp (0/1) is the Lawton-Brody dependency score rather than the administered response: each domain offers 3-5 instrument levels that collapse to able/unable, so option_text names the scored category and lists the levels sharing it instead of a single literal option label. The study’s data supplement also records only the total IADL score, so the item-to-domain mapping follows the standard Lawton & Brody (1969) ordering rather than an explicit map, and item text comes from the canonical instrument











Warningamerican_multiracial_face





Each item is one photograph rated on one attribute, and the item codes are arbitrary integers assigned when the study’s 19 separate rating files were stacked – they carry no meaning and must not be read as an item order. item_text is therefore a constructed description of the stimulus rather than transcribed text; the verbatim rating question is the section_prompt. The AMFD PhotoID named in item_text is not stated in the source materials and was recovered by matching per-face rating means against the published norming table, and 9 faces (171 items) were never released in the AMFD and so carry no PhotoID. Only scale points 1 and 7 were labelled in the original survey, so option_text is blank for 2-6. Separately, the table has no Black-prototypicality ratings for the smiling photographs: the source repository provides them, but the IRW processing script does not read that file











Warningan_2020_efl_self_regulated





The table name signals one instrument but the table pools three administered in the same survey: the TSELSS strategy items (Q1-Q26), an English-learning enjoyment/environment block (Q27-Q33), and a 16-item English language self-efficacy questionnaire (Q34-Q49). Item text is the original Chinese from the study’s own data file. Only the two endpoints of the 7-point scale are labelled in that file, so option_text is blank for values 2-6











Warninganjum_2022_gad7





The IRW table covers 6 of the GAD-7’s 7 items: item 1 (“Feeling nervous, anxious, or on edge”) is present in the study’s data file but was not included in the IRW release. Two item wordings and the response anchors follow that file’s own labels, which differ from canonical GAD-7 wording – “not being able to sleep or control worrying” for “stop or control”, “hart to sit still” for “hard”, and “More than half of the days” for “More than half the days”. The instructions are the canonical GAD-7 stem; the data file carries none











WarningAOMT_BR_SF_EDPANAB_Geiger_2021_AOT





The table carries 14 item codes for a 10-item scale. AOT3_rev, AOT5_rev, AOT7_rev and AOT8_rev are reverse-coded duplicates of AOT3, AOT5, AOT7 and AOT8 rather than additional items – the same statement, with the response options in reverse order – so they carry their parent item’s text and reversed option_text











WarningAOMT_BR_SF_EDPANAB_Geiger_2021_BRS





The table name signals the Bullshit Receptivity Scale alone, but it combines that scale’s 10 items (BSR) with the 10 motivational-quotation control statements (MOT) from the same study; both blocks were rated on the same “profoundness” scale











Warningarnulf_2022_general_knowledge





The general-knowledge test was open-answer, so participants did not choose from the options shown here: option_text gives the Correct/Incorrect scoring labels the study’s data file attaches to 0 and 1. Item text is verbatim from that file, including its “principle street for finance in New York” where the paper’s prose reads “principal”











Warningarora2025_blueq_synchronous





The study’s data file records only numeric codes, so the response anchors and the section prompt are taken from the published BLUE-Q instrument. That instrument’s prompt describes a “face-to-face component”, while this study administered the synchronous sessions as online workshops – the item text itself, which is verbatim from the study’s own spreadsheet, refers to “face-to-face online workshops”











Warningart





The Author Recognition Test presents a checklist of names with no printed response labels, so option_text (“Checked”/“Not checked”) describes the check-box rather than quoting the instrument, and item_text repeats the author name shown on the checklist. Only the 50 real-author items are in the IRW table; the 50 foils were dropped upstream. The name “T.S. Elliot” is kept as the source data spells it (canonically “T. S. Eliot”)











Warningartistic_preferences





The table name describes only the first of three instruments administered in the same session: items 1-30 are the Artistic Preferences Scales, items 31-40 the Ten Item Personality Inventory, and items 41-56 a 16-word vocabulary check list. Items 1-30 have no text stem at all – each is a pair of paintings, shown as images, that the respondent chooses between and rates the strength of the preference; the images are distributed with the source dataset. Only the two extreme points of that 1-5 scale carry anchors, so option_text is blank for 2-4











Warningarzamoncunill_2023_epq_clinical





None of the item text here is the wording respondents read. item_text is the short category descriptor the study’s supplement gives for each item number (“Editable agenda”, “Videoconference”), which names what the item is about rather than quoting it. The study ran a 43-item pretest pool but published full item wording, in Spanish, only for the 26 items kept in its final questionnaire, while this table holds all 22 clinical-care items of the pretest pool – so 10 of the 22 have no published wording in any language, and the descriptor is the only text that exists for them. The study’s own data file carries no variable or value labels, so there is no better source; the item numbers themselves are matched exactly, only the words are substitutes











Warningaudretsch_2021_entrepreneurial_ecosystems





Item text is the untruncated form of the study data file’s variable labels, recovered from its Stata do-file because the .dta labels are cut off at Stata’s 80-character cap. For the ee_quality item the paper’s own section 4.2 quotes a different wording (“There is a strong focus on growth-oriented and productive entrepreneurship activity in my region (city)”) from the data-file label that is shipped here (“There is a strong entrepreneurship ecosystem (EE) in my region (city)”). Several labels are ungrammatical or unclosed in the source and are transcribed as they stand. Only the endpoints of the 1-7 scale (1 = very weak, 7 = very strong) are documented, so the intermediate options are blank











Warningautonomysupport_mokken





The item “Decide” is reverse-worded in the original questionnaire, but the responses in this table are the raw, unreversed scores, so the same anchors apply to it as to every other item. Item text is the English rendering the mokken package documents for a questionnaire administered in Dutch. Only the two extreme anchors are documented (1 = not at all/never, 5 = certainly/always)











Warningavilesgonzalez2019_ces





Item text comes from the study’s SPSS file, which stores the English Caring Efficacy Scale wording even though the respondents were Italian nurses, so it is not what they read. Several typographical errors in those labels are preserved here as the source has them – one item is missing its opening “If”, another reads “Ioften”, and several begin with a lowercase “i”











Warningbaaziz_2023_sms2





The text shown for item 16 is probably not the item respondents answered, and should not be used as the wording of that item. The paper prints “So that others praise me for what I do” at position 16, which is external-regulation content, but in the data item 16 behaves as amotivation: it correlates 0.88-0.90 with items 17 and 18, the other two amotivation items, and essentially zero (0.02, 0.04, -0.03) with the three external-regulation items 13-15. Position 16 in the SMS-II is an amotivation item, so the paper’s table appears to misprint its wording; the printed text is shipped here unchanged rather than substituted with a guess. Item text throughout is the paper’s own English back-translation – the questionnaire was administered in Arabic, and the Arabic wording printed alongside it is not reproduced here. Only the endpoints of the 7-point scale are documented, so options 2-6 are blank











Warningbaka2023_bpnsf





The response anchors here are given in the OPPOSITE direction to the study data file’s own value labels, which state 1 = Strongly agree through 7 = Strongly disagree. The data contradict that: scoring the file as labelled would make every need-satisfaction item correlate negatively with the same respondents’ work engagement, measured on an unambiguous 0-6 Never..Always scale. Sorted by item content, all 12 satisfaction items correlate +0.28 to +0.40 with that engagement score and all 12 frustration items -0.03 to -0.22, which is only possible if the scale runs 1 = Strongly disagree to 7 = Strongly agree, as shipped. Item text is the administered Polish, with the source file’s typos retained











Warningbaka2023_jcs





Item stems are in Polish as administered, but the response anchors carried by the study’s data file are English glosses rather than the Polish wording participants saw











Warningbaka2023_olbi





Only 8 of the published OLBI’s 16 items are present in the study’s data file, and those 8 are what this table covers. Item stems are in Polish as administered, but the response anchors carried by the data file are English glosses rather than the Polish wording participants saw











Warningbaka2023_uwes





Item stems are in Polish as administered, but the response anchors carried by the study’s data file are English glosses rather than the Polish wording participants saw











Warningbakker_2020_rses





The item codes for this table must not be read as item content. Seven of the ten columns in the study’s SPSS file carry a variable label that contradicts the column name, and the data show the labels are the reliable half: the column named goodqualities303 is labelled “All in all, I am inclined to feel that I am a failure” and averages 1.47 on a 1-4 Strongly Disagree..Strongly Agree scale, while nogood302 is labelled “I feel that I have a number of good qualities” and averages 3.27. Every negatively-worded label sits at the floor and every positively-worded one at the ceiling, which a positively-worded self-esteem item could not do in a general sample. Read in column order the labels reproduce a standard circulated administration order of the scale, so the names appear to have been assigned by numbering the columns in Rosenberg’s original order without noticing the form was permuted. The text shipped here follows the labels; join on the item code and read the text, not the code. Responses are stored raw and unreversed. Note also that the paper’s Methods states the scale ran 1 = strongly agree to 4 = strongly disagree, the reverse of the data file’s own value labels; the data follow the file











Warningbang_2023_self_esteem





The item order in this table was reconstructed, not read from any key, and the item text is not what respondents saw. Neither the study’s data file (bare codes S1-S10) nor the paper ties any code to an item, so the shipped text is the canonical English Rosenberg Self-Esteem Scale wording placed in an order inferred from the reverse-keying pattern in the raw responses; the study administered the Korean version (Jon, 1974), whose wording is not reproduced anywhere. What the data establish is each item’s polarity: S1, S2, S4, S6 and S7 intercorrelate positively (+0.31 to +0.73) and S3, S5, S9 and S10 form the opposing block, which rules out the scale’s original item numbering, and S8 is identifiable by its distinctive near-zero correlation with the positive block. What they do not establish is the order within each polarity block, so a swap between two same-polarity items – S1 and S2, say – is not excluded











Warningbartoli_2022_badge_notifications





This table records a single-click behavioural task rather than a questionnaire. Each participant saw one home screen of 15 app icons with a badge notification on one app and made a single click, so resp = 100 marks the one app that participant clicked first and 0 the other fourteen. The response-option text is descriptive; the task offered no labelled options. The item text gives each app’s conventional name, with the Italian default-app labels left as administered











Warningbeck_2021_iesr





resp values 1-4 are category indices, not scores. The study used the German IES-R (Maercker & Schuetzwohl, 1998), whose four anchors are ueberhaupt nicht / selten / manchmal / oft and whose traditional scoring weights that version prints are 0, 1, 3 and 5 – so summing resp gives a different scale from the published one. Item text is that German form verbatim, including its pre-1996 orthography











Warningbeck_2021_pss10





The PSS-10 was administered in German, but the study names no German translation, so the item text shown here is the original English wording rather than what respondents read. Items 4, 5, 7 and 8 are stored unreversed and must be reversed before scoring, and the response coding is the canonical 0-4 shifted by one (1 = Never … 5 = Very often)











Warningbitew_2020_lte





Item text is the study’s own abbreviated SPSS variable labels (“self illness”, “family death”), not the administered wording, which was in Amharic and was never published. Canonical Life Events Questionnaire wording was deliberately not substituted because this version departs from it: items 8-11 are reordered relative to the original sequence, and item 12 (intimate partner violence) is not an LTE-Q item at all











Warningbitew_2020_osss3





Item wording is the canonical English OSSS-3 rather than the study’s administered Amharic version. One caveat on the mapping: item 1’s variable label in the source file reads “others worry for me”, which does not obviously correspond to the canonical item-1 content about how many people you can count on. It is identified as item 1 by its response structure instead – it is the only one of the three offering four categories rather than five, which is the instrument’s own signature, and the file’s total column equals the sum of the three items for every case











Warningbitew_2020_phq9





Item wording is the canonical English PHQ-9; the study administered a locally validated Amharic translation whose exact wording is not published. The mapping to those canonical items is confirmed by the source file’s own numbered symptom labels and by the paper’s reported per-item means











Warningbitew_2020_self_efficacy





This table holds 9 of the General Self-Efficacy Scale’s 10 items, and its item codes are offset by one: SEFFICAn is GSE item n+1, so SEFFICA1 is GSE item 2. The source file does contain GSE item 1, under a differently-named column, but it was not shipped to the IRW. The response anchors are the authors’ own shorthand for the GSE’s Not at all true…Exactly true scale











Warningbrederecke_2020_sis





Items 4 and 9 are stored reverse-coded in the source data, and the option text here follows that stored direction: for those two items resp = 1 is “strongly agree” and 5 is “strongly disagree”, while the other nine run 1 = strongly disagree to 5 = strongly agree. This is stated by the study’s own file, which names those two columns “SIS Item 4 recoded” and “SIS Item 9 recoded” – they are the scale’s two negatively-worded items. Item text gives the English wording followed by the German actually administered











Warningbroadband_inventories





The instructions, quoted verbatim from the test’s own page, describe a five-point scale, but the items were administered on the seven-point Strongly disagree..Strongly agree scale that resp 1-7 encodes. The item wording is otherwise verbatim from the source codebook, including its typos (item 18 reads “when Im feeling badly”)











Warningbuczel_2022_inoculation_belief





Each of these six items covers six different question wordings. The study counterbalanced six scenarios across participants, so the sentence any one participant read depends on which scenario they saw; item_text therefore names the item’s condition and quotes one scenario’s wording as an example rather than presenting one participant’s version as the item. Note also that the response scale displayed to participants ran 0-10 while resp is stored as 1-11, so the option text carries the displayed number and is deliberately not equal to resp











Warningbukurov_2022_sf36





Item and option wording is the public-domain English RAND 36-Item Health Survey. The study administered a Serbian-language SF-36, so this is canonical text rather than what participants read. The mapping to those canonical items is firm: the source file labels every column with its item, and the per-item response formats match the instrument’s mixed structure exactly (5 levels for items 1, 2, 20, 22 and 32-36; 3 for items 3-12; 2 for 13-19; 6 for 21 and 23-31)











Warningburkert_2019_whoqol_bref





Items LQ3 (pain), LQ4 (dependence on medical treatment) and LQ26 (negative feelings) are stored already reverse-coded, so for those three resp = 5 is the most favourable answer, and the option text here reflects that stored direction rather than the order printed on the questionnaire – which the source file’s own value labels still describe. The data settle it: those three items correlate positively (+0.18 to +0.46) with unambiguously positive-keyed items such as overall quality of life and mobility, and 52% of respondents sit at LQ3 = 5, which is only interpretable as “not at all hindered by pain” in a general-population sample











Warningbusch_2022_course_alleviate





These are the checkbox options of a single select-all-that-apply survey question, not independently administered items: resp = 1 means the respondent ticked that aspect and 0 means they did not, so a 0 records the absence of a tick rather than substantive disagreement. The question was shown only to the respondents who reported depression symptoms while taking online science courses











Warningbrederecke_2020_phq4





The item text is the study data file’s own terse English variable labels (“little interest or pleasure in your activities”), which are neither the German wording the instrument was administered in nor the canonical PHQ-4 phrasing. The response options are that file’s English labels too, and they likewise differ from the published PHQ-4 anchors – “On single days” where the instrument reads “Several days”. The instructions line is the canonical PHQ-4 stem, which the data file does not carry











Warningburgess_2025_soas





The item codes are non-contiguous – SOAS5, 7, 9, 10, 11 and 12 – because they refer to positions in the 13-item version administered in this study, of which these six were retained in the final scale. The study’s data file carries no variable or value labels, so the item text and that numbering come from the paper’s own item table rather than from the data. In this study the items were read aloud to children who were shown a fixed object, so the published instrument’s opening line asking the respondent to choose and write down an object did not apply and is not included here











Warningbrain_hemisphere





The instructions field describes the response scale rather than quoting an instruction shown to participants; the source dataset documents the scale but publishes no participant-facing instruction text. Only three of the five scale points were labelled (1 = Disagree, 3 = Neutral, 5 = Agree), so the option text is blank at 2 and 4. Note also that this 2015-16 dataset is the 20-item version of the scale; the version currently offered online has 24 items











Warningbusch_2023_stigma





Despite the table name, these items are not stigma ratings. They are the participants’ own binary self-reports of concealable identities – LGBQ+, depression, anxiety, low SES, first-generation status, academic struggle, disability, community-college transfer – while the study’s actual 4-point perceived-stigma measure is not in the IRW table at all. Six of the eight items share the identical stem “I most closely identify as”, so the item content lives entirely in the response options. For two items the binary 0 collapses several source options (for example mid and upper income both map to 0), and the option text joins those source options verbatim; “Decline to state” responses are dropped rather than coded











Warningbutt_2022_cognitive_absorption





The study’s data file contains four of the six Cognitive Absorption items – CA3 and CA5 were dropped by the authors – and it carries no variable labels for them, so the wording here comes from the appendix questionnaire, which lists the six items in order without codes. The alignment is therefore by position within that block











Warningbutt_2022_institutional_factors





Eleven of the appendix’s thirteen Institutional Factors items are in the data; IF3 and IF11 are absent from the study’s own file and are not shipped. The data file gives no variable labels for these columns, so the wording comes from the appendix questionnaire by position within the block. One source typo was corrected: the appendix prints “students ’questions” with a misplaced opening quote, shipped here as “students’ questions”











Warningbutt_2022_actual_usage





This two-item scale does not use the questionnaire’s 1-7 agreement scale: each item has its own response anchors – a frequency scale for one and hours per week for the other – so instructions is blank because the block’s shared instruction does not apply











Warningbuzgova_2023_rses





The item numbering here is an assumption that could not be independently confirmed. The study’s data file carries no variable or value labels of any kind and the paper reproduces no items, so the text is the canonical English Rosenberg Self-Esteem Scale mapped on the basis that RSESn is Rosenberg item n. That assumption is known to fail for this instrument: in bakker_2020_rses the columns were numbered in canonical order while the administered form was permuted. Here the responses are stored already reverse-scored – every inter-item correlation is positive – so the keying-polarity check that caught the other case cannot be run. One position does have positive support: RSES8 has both the lowest mean and the lowest item-rest correlation, the known signature of Rosenberg item 8 (“I wish I could have more respect for myself”). Positions 1-7, 9 and 10 rest on the numbering alone. The scale is also stored pre-reversed, so the same anchors apply to every item











Warningbuzgova_2023_soc





Item text is the canonical English SOC-13; the study was Czech and its translation is not published in the paper or the data file, which carries no labels of any kind. The responses are stored already reverse-scored, so the option text for the five reverse-worded items (1, 2, 3, 7 and 10) is flipped relative to the printed instrument. Note also a discrepancy with the paper: it reports Cronbach’s alpha of 0.92 for this scale, while the released data give 0.765 with corrected item-total correlations of 0.29-0.53











Warningbuzgova_2023_gai





Item text is the canonical English Geriatric Anxiety Inventory; the study was Czech and its translation is not published, and the data file carries no labels of any kind. The mapping of code to item is supported but not settled: the instrument’s published three-factor structure reproduces for 15 of the 20 items, with the three purely somatic items all behaving as expected, while five cognitive-versus-arousal items are ambiguous











Warningbuzgova_2023_gds





Item text is the canonical English GDS-15; the study was Czech and its translation is not published in the paper or the data file, which carries no labels of any kind. The responses are stored already scored rather than raw, so resp = 1 always marks the depression-consistent answer and the option text follows that stored direction rather than the yes/no order printed on the questionnaire











Warningbuzgova_2023_lsita





This table is the 12-item short form of the LSITA, and the item text is the canonical English wording – the study was Czech and its translation is published nowhere accessible, the data file carries no labels, and the companion validation paper is paywalled. Items 2, 4, 5 and 6 are stored already reversed, so their option text is flipped relative to the printed instrument; the raw column sum reproduces the paper’s published total exactly, which is what establishes that











Warningcacciatore_2021_crisis_care_satisfaction





The resp values are not the survey’s own choice numbering. The questionnaire numbered its options 1 = Extremely satisfied down to 6 = N/A, while the IRW values are the processing script’s recoding into ascending satisfaction, and the “N/A” responses are dropped rather than kept as a level. Item text is the matrix row label and the shared stem is recorded once in instructions; respondents rated only the care providers they actually encountered, which is why the number of responses varies widely across items











Warningchen_2022_sasc





Despite the table name, SASC here is the Smartphone Addiction Scale for College Students (SAS-C; Su et al., 2014), measuring problematic smartphone use – not the Social Anxiety Scale for Children. The survey was administered in Chinese and the wording shown is the depositors’ own English item labels from the SPSS file, as no Chinese original is published with the dataset











Warningcriticalperiod_syntax





Six of the 95 items (q1, q2, q3, q5, q6 and q7) are sentence-to-picture matching items whose two answer choices are pictures. The source publishes those pictures only as figures, never as text, so the option_text on those twelve rows is a machine-generated description of each picture rather than source wording – every one is prefixed [machine-generated image description] to make that unmistakable, and it is the only text in this table not transcribed from the source. Which picture belongs to which response is not guessed: the study’s supplement prints an answer key naming the correct panel for each of the six, and because these are two-alternative forced choices, resp = 1 means the respondent chose that panel and resp = 0 means they chose the other. The remaining 89 items are grammaticality judgments and carry no option_text at all – there resp is scored accuracy on a “choose all that apply” question, so no single option was chosen and any label would be invented. Separately, Question 10’s four response options are printed in the supplement under a duplicated “c.” label (a, b, c, c, with no “d.”), so item q10_4 is identified as the fourth printed option, “What old are you?”, by its position and by the answer key’s grammaticality value; “How old are you?” (option 3) is grammatical in every dialect and is not in the table











Warningdepression_anxiety_stress





This table pools three instruments administered in one openpsychometrics session, not the DASS alone: items 1-42 are the DASS-42, items 43-52 are the Ten Item Personality Inventory, and items 53-68 are a 16-word vocabulary checklist scored 0/1 (VCL6 “cuivocal”, VCL9 “florted” and VCL12 “verdid” are not real words and were included as a validity check). The item codes are bare integers assigned by the processing script and carry no content of their own











Warningftna_kasper_2022





The “items” in this table are whole-subject examination grades (Mathematics, Kiswahili and so on), not individual exam questions. Note also that the three core subjects reuse one item code across both waves, even though wave 0 is the primary-school PSLE and wave 1 the secondary-school FTNA – so the same code refers to a different examination in each wave











Warninggeography





Each item is a place on an outline map rather than a questionnaire item, and its item_text is the place name from the source archive’s own lookup table with the place type appended in parentheses – an annotation added here, not part of the source name – because 46 place names are shared by two different places. The task presented no fixed answer options, so option_text labels the 0/1 correctness score rather than transcribing anything the learner saw











Warningriasec





Only items 1-48 of this table are the RIASEC interest inventory the table is named for. Items 49-58 are the Ten Item Personality Inventory and items 59-74 a 16-word vocabulary checklist, administered in the same session, and the three use different response scales (1-5, 1-7 and 0/1 respectively)











Warningsapa_personality





17 of the 696 items ship the SAPA item dictionary’s abbreviated shorthand – bracketed or elided text – rather than the full sentence the participant read; the remaining 679 carry the full wording. Item text and the six response anchors both come from the SAPA-Project data release’s own item dictionary (ItemInfo696) and code book

title: Data
text: This page has two tools:

title: Data
Data
The Item Response Warehouse (IRW)
The Item Response Warehouse (IRW)
text:
Why the IRW exists
Researchers who study measurement — in education, psychology, and related fields — need real data to test and compare their methods. That data already exists in large quantities. But it is scattered across many studies, stored in many different formats, and often hard to reuse because of unclear documentation or licensing.
This is a well-known problem. The research community has articulated a shared standard for solving it: data should be FAIR — Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable (Wilkinson et al., 2016). Other fields put these principles into practice by building shared, standardized data resources. In computer science, the ImageNet collection of labeled images gave researchers a common benchmark and helped drive rapid progress in AI. Genetics and neuroscience built similar shared resources for their own data.
The Item Response Warehouse (IRW) applies the same FAIR principles to item response data. It brings together hundreds of existing datasets and reshapes them into one common format — so that a method tested on one dataset can easily be tested on hundreds of others.

title: The Item Response Warehouse (IRW)
text:
What is in the IRW
The IRW contains hundreds of datasets (“tables”), each one a collection of individual responses. A response is generated whenever some person (or other unit) responds to some item (or other probe). Examples include:

Student answers on education and ability tests
Survey items measuring personality or attitudes
Ratings assigned by human raters
Any other setting involving repeated responses to a set of measurement probes

Every dataset in the IRW is designed to be:

Findable. Each dataset comes with pre-computed metadata — participant and item counts, response density, subject area, and other descriptive tags — so datasets can be located and filtered without downloading them first.
Accessible. Every dataset can be retrieved through the web browser or the irw package, using a free account.
Interoperable. Each dataset is reshaped into the same simple long-format structure (described below), so the same analysis code can run across many datasets with little or no modification.
Reusable. Each dataset is openly licensed, its origin is documented, and the code used to convert it into the IRW format is public.

Datasets vary widely in size (from a few hundred responses to many millions) and in response type (yes/no items, multi-category ratings, partial-credit scores, and more). Each dataset also comes with pre-computed metadata — number of participants, number of items, response density, subject area, and other descriptive tags — so that researchers can find relevant datasets without first downloading and processing all of them.

title: The Item Response Warehouse (IRW)
text:
The data standard

Every IRW dataset is reshaped into long format: one row per response. At minimum, each row has three pieces of information:







Column
Meaning




id
Who (or what) produced the response — typically a person


item
Which measurement probe produced the response — typically a question or task


resp
The response itself, stored as an ordinal score



Example:

When a dataset includes extra information — response time, rater identity, covariates such as age — that information is stored in additional, consistently named columns. This one simple structure covers a huge range of measurement situations, which is what makes it possible to write analysis code once and apply it across the entire warehouse.
The full technical specification of the standard is available at itemresponsewarehouse.org/standard.html. Related, more specialized standards also exist for item text, pairwise-competition data, and nominal (unordered category) responses.

title: The Item Response Warehouse (IRW)
text:
How to use it
There are three ways to get IRW data, depending on how much you want to automate.
1. Browse in the web browser Explore datasets and their metadata directly on the IRW data browser — no account needed. Downloading a full dataset requires a free Redivis account, since that is the platform that hosts the underlying data.
2. Use the irw package (recommended) The irw package, available for both R and Python, gives simple functions for finding, filtering, and downloading data.
# R
devtools::install_github("itemresponsewarehouse/Rpkg")
library(irw)

irw_info()                     # overview of the IRW
irw_list_tables()              # list all available tables
irw_filter(var = "rt")         # find tables that include response times
df <- irw_fetch("4thgrade_math_sirt")   # download one table
# Python
# pip install "git+https://github.com/itemresponsewarehouse/Python-pkg.git"
import irw

irw.info()
irw.list_tables()
irw.filter(var="rt")
df = irw.fetch("4thgrade_math_sirt")
The first time you use the package, you will be asked to log in with a free Redivis account. After that, one line of code downloads any dataset directly into R or Python. From there, the data is ready for analysis with standard software — for example, item response theory or factor analysis packages.
3. Use the Redivis client libraries directly For lower-level or non-R/Python workflows, the data can also be accessed through Redivis’s own R and Python client libraries. See the Getting Started guide for details.

Beyond downloading data
The IRW project also includes:

A growing set of vignettes — worked examples applying classic and new measurement methods across many IRW datasets at once
Training resources and problem sets for teaching psychometrics with real data
A contribution process for researchers who want to add their own datasets to the warehouse

title: The Item Response Warehouse (IRW)
text:
Learn more

Domingue et al. (2025). An introduction to the Item Response Warehouse (IRW): A resource for enhancing data usage in psychometrics. Behavior Research Methods. doi:10.3758/s13428-025-02796-y
Nadela, Lee, Jain, Gupta, Zhang & Domingue (2026). The Item Response Warehouse: What It Is, How to Use It, and Targets for Potential Improvements. Chinese/English Journal of Educational Measurement and Evaluation. doi:10.59863/CIJG4549
Wilkinson et al. (2016). The FAIR Guiding Principles for scientific data management and stewardship. Scientific Data. doi:10.1038/sdata.2016.18
Website: itemresponsewarehouse.org
Code: github.com/itemresponsewarehouse

If you use IRW data in your work, please cite the original data (we have provided functionality for doing so). It would also be great if you cared to cite the introductory paper above.

Questions, feedback, or want to contribute a dataset? Visit the Contact page or open an issue on GitHub.

title: Contributing data to the IRW
text: We welcome contribution of new datasets to the IRW!

title: Contributing data to the IRW
text:
Contributing data

If you would like to contribute data, please fill out the (brief) form here.
We will take information about any data that you think may be worth including in the IRW. Inclusion will be easier if the data is already in a format consistent with the IRW data standard. Below we provide information on how to construct such a dataset.

title: Contributing data to the IRW
text:
Constructing an IRW-compliant dataset
Below are critical instructions for formatting data for the IRW. More details are available here.

Numeric values of a response should be meaningful. For example, missing values cannot be coded as numbers (e.g., -9).
Please check that the id and item identifiers have an appropriate number of unique values.
Additional data elements (e.g., rt, date, wave, rater, qmatrix) should all be formatted as specified above.
If there are multiple scales available, the responses need to be split into multiple files (one per scale). If multiple groups are assessed via the same scale, these data can be put into a single file (if desired, a column indicating group membership can be added).

While we have tried to offer generic guidance on formatting data to the IRW standard, there are innumerable idiosyncrasies that may merit additional conversation. To discuss specific issues associated with formatting your data to the IRW standard, please feel free to reach out to us at itemresponsewarehouse@stanford.edu. We would be happy to talk more! You can also use the IRW Dataset Builder that will help port data to the IRW data standard if you like.

title: Overview of the IRW Data Standards
text: Data standards are an essential mechanism of increasing reusability and interoperability of data amongst researchers. As such, they play a critical role in increasing the extent to which science is FAIR (findable, accessible, interoperable, reusable). The IRW contains several different ‘branches’ that utilize distinct data standards. We focus here on describing the differences between these data standards (with pointers to complete descriptions of the specific standards).

title: Overview of the IRW Data Standards
text:
The data standards
In all cases, we are interested in cross-classified responses. The differences amongst the standards pertain to the nature of either the cross-classification or the response.

The core IRW data standard: Responses here are from a probe used to measure some trait of some object. Note that the probes and the objects are categorically different. Further, the responses are ordinal. Additional detail can be found here.
The ‘competitions’ data standard: Responses here are ordinal but from direct comparison/competition between the entities that we are interested in measuring (e.g., there is no categorically distinct probe). See here for more details.
The ‘nominal’ data standard: Similar to the core data standard, a probe is being used to measure some trait but the responses are nominal rather than ordinal. See more here.

Note that we also have a branch which contains simulated or synthetic data formatted to meet the core standard.

title: Item-Level Heterogeneous Treatment Effects
text:
Many RCTs in education, economics, and health research use psychometric instruments — tests, surveys, symptom checklists — as outcome measures. A standard analysis sums responses into a single score and estimates the average treatment effect (ATE) on that score. But the individual items of the instrument may not respond equally to treatment. An item that directly targets the intervention’s content may show a large positive effect while an unrelated item shows none.
This item-level variation is called item-level heterogeneous treatment effects (IL-HTE) (Gilbert, Himmelsbach, et al. 2025). Beyond masking item-level variation, IL-HTE has a less obvious consequence for causal identification. When item-level effects are correlated with item difficulty, a conventional treatment-by-covariate interaction model — the standard tool for asking “who benefits most?” — can produce biased estimates even when no true person-level heterogeneity exists. Gilbert, Miratrix, et al. (2025) prove this analytically and demonstrate it through simulation. We illustrate both insights below using RCT datasets from the IRW.

title: Item-Level Heterogeneous Treatment Effects
text:
Many RCTs in education, economics, and health research use psychometric instruments — tests, surveys, symptom checklists — as outcome measures. A standard analysis sums responses into a single score and estimates the average treatment effect (ATE) on that score. But the individual items of the instrument may not respond equally to treatment. An item that directly targets the intervention’s content may show a large positive effect while an unrelated item shows none.
This item-level variation is called item-level heterogeneous treatment effects (IL-HTE) (Gilbert, Himmelsbach, et al. 2025). Beyond masking item-level variation, IL-HTE has a less obvious consequence for causal identification. When item-level effects are correlated with item difficulty, a conventional treatment-by-covariate interaction model — the standard tool for asking “who benefits most?” — can produce biased estimates even when no true person-level heterogeneity exists. Gilbert, Miratrix, et al. (2025) prove this analytically and demonstrate it through simulation. We illustrate both insights below using RCT datasets from the IRW.

title: Item-Level Heterogeneous Treatment Effects
text:
Data and methods

Dataset selection
We use IRW tables that record a binary treat indicator and have at least 100 participants (irw_filter(var = "treat", n_participants = c(100, Inf))). For datasets with a wave column (multiple follow-up waves), only wave 1 is used. Items are restricted to those with exactly two response categories; datasets with fewer than three dichotomous items after that restriction are dropped. Respondent counts are downsampled to at most 5,000 IDs for large datasets to keep model fitting tractable.


The IL-HTE model
Formally, if the log-odds of a correct response for item \(i\) by person \(j\) follows
\[
\begin{align}
    \text{logit}(\Pr(Y_{ij} = 1)) = \eta_{ij} &= \theta_j + b_{i} + \zeta_i T_j \\
    \theta_j &= \beta_0 + \beta_1 T_j + \varepsilon_j \\
    \begin{bmatrix}
        b_i \\
        \zeta_{i}
    \end{bmatrix}
     &\sim N\left(\begin{bmatrix}
         0 \\ 0
     \end{bmatrix},\begin{bmatrix}
         \sigma^2_b & \rho\sigma_b\sigma_\zeta \\
         \rho\sigma_b\sigma_\zeta & \sigma^2_\zeta
     \end{bmatrix}\right) \\
    \varepsilon_j &\sim N(0, \sigma^2_\theta)
\end{align}
\]
then \(\zeta_i\) is the residual treatment effect on item \(i\) above and beyond the overall ATE \(\beta_1\). When the variance \(\sigma_\zeta^2 > 0\), items respond heterogeneously to treatment. In lme4 notation this is:
glmer(resp ~ treat + (1|id) + (treat|item), family = binomial)
We fit this model to each dataset, extract empirical Bayes estimates of the item-specific effects \(\hat\beta_1 + \hat\zeta_i\), and standardize by \(\hat\sigma_\theta\) — the person-level SD from a baseline random-intercepts model with no treatment slope — so that effects are comparable across datasets. Statistical significance of \(\sigma_\zeta\) uses a likelihood-ratio test against that baseline model, with the standard boundary correction of halving the reported p-value (the null variance of zero sits at the edge of the parameter space).


Model comparison for the identification problem
We illustrate the identification problem empirically by fitting two additional models per dataset, wherever a pretest covariate is available:

M_B (constant item effects + person HTE): resp ~ treat + cov + treat:cov + (1|item) + (1|id)
M_C (flexible EIRM — IL-HTE + person HTE): resp ~ treat + cov + treat:cov + (treat|item) + (1|id)

where cov is the standardized pretest score: std_baseline where the dataset provides it, or otherwise whichever cov_-prefixed column is most correlated with the response in the control arm alone. Datasets with no usable pretest covariate contribute to the item-level-effects analysis above but are excluded from this comparison. The \(\hat\beta_3\) coefficient on treat:cov represents the treatment-by-covariate interaction; M_B estimates it without allowing for IL-HTE, M_C estimates it alongside IL-HTE.

title: Item-Level Heterogeneous Treatment Effects
text:
Results

Item-level treatment effects
The ATE \(\hat\beta_1\) is shown as a large point; individual item effects as small points. Datasets are ordered by ATE. Color encodes whether the IL-HTE variance \(\sigma_\zeta\) is statistically significant.


Code
tab_order <- summary_df |> arrange(ate_std) |> pull(tab)

plot_df <- item_df |>
  left_join(summary_df |> select(tab, ate_std, sig_il_hte), by = "tab") |>
  mutate(
    y_pos     = as.integer(factor(tab, levels = tab_order)),
    sig_label = if_else(sig_il_hte, "Significant", "Not significant"),
    color_val = if_else(sig_il_hte, irw_blue, irw_red)
  )

ate_df <- summary_df |>
  mutate(
    y_pos     = as.integer(factor(tab, levels = tab_order)),
    sig_label = if_else(sig_il_hte, "Significant", "Not significant"),
    color_val = if_else(sig_il_hte, irw_blue, irw_red),
    hover_text = paste0(
      "<b>", tab, "</b><br>",
      "ATE: ", round(ate_std, 3), " SD<br>",
      "σζ: ", round(sigma_zeta_std, 3), " SD<br>",
      "ρ: ", round(rho, 2), "<br>",
      "Items: ", n_items, "<br>",
      "N: ", n_persons, "<br>",
      "Sig. IL-HTE: ", sig_il_hte
    )
  )

fig <- plot_ly() |>
  add_trace(
    data       = plot_df,
    x          = ~total_std,
    y          = ~y_pos,
    type       = "scatter",
    mode       = "markers",
    marker     = list(size = 4, opacity = 0.4),
    color      = ~sig_label,
    colors     = c("Significant" = irw_blue, "Not significant" = irw_red),
    hoverinfo  = "none",
    showlegend = TRUE
  ) |>
  add_trace(
    data       = ate_df,
    x          = ~ate_std,
    y          = ~y_pos,
    type       = "scatter",
    mode       = "markers",
    marker     = list(size = 10, line = list(width = 1, color = "white")),
    color      = ~sig_label,
    colors     = c("Significant" = irw_blue, "Not significant" = irw_red),
    text       = ~hover_text,
    hoverinfo  = "text",
    showlegend = FALSE
  ) |>
  layout(
    height = max(400, nrow(summary_df) * 14),
    xaxis = list(title = "Item-specific treatment effect (SDs)",
                 zeroline = TRUE, zerolinecolor = "#aaa", zerolinewidth = 1),
    yaxis = list(title = "", showticklabels = FALSE, showgrid = FALSE),
    legend = list(orientation = "h", x = 0, y = -0.05),
    margin = list(l = 20)
  )

fig








Figure 1: Empirical Bayes estimates of item-specific treatment effects, standardized by σ_θ. Small points: individual item effects (β₁ + ζ̂ᵢ)/σ_θ. Hover over the large dot to see dataset details.




Across 70 datasets, 40 show statistically significant IL-HTE (\(p < 0.05\)). In datasets with wide spreads of item effects, a single-number ATE obscures meaningful variation in which aspects of the outcome respond to the intervention — information that would be invisible in a sum-score analysis.


The identification problem
Gilbert, Miratrix, et al. (2025) show analytically that when item-level effects are correlated with item difficulty (\(\rho \ne 0\)), two distinct data-generating processes — (1) true person-level HTE via a treatment × pretest interaction, and (2) item-level HTE correlated with item difficulty — produce identical patterns in sum-score outcomes. A model that omits IL-HTE therefore cannot distinguish between these processes and will produce biased estimates of the treatment-by-covariate interaction.
Specifically, when \(\rho > 0\) (easier items respond more strongly to treatment), treatment “stretches” the item difficulty distribution — the ratio \(\sigma_b^\text{treat}/\sigma_b^\text{ctrl}\) exceeds 1 — and the constant-item model attributes this variation to a spurious negative treatment-by-pretest interaction.


Code
id_df <- summary_df |>
  filter(!is.na(delta_beta3)) |>
  mutate(
    hover_text = paste0(
      "<b>", tab, "</b><br>",
      "Δβ₃: ", round(delta_beta3, 3), "<br>",
      "SD ratio: ", round(sd_ratio, 3), "<br>",
      "ρ: ", round(rho, 2), "<br>",
      "Items: ", n_items, "<br>",
      "N: ", n_persons
    )
  )

plot_ly(id_df,
  x         = ~sd_ratio,
  y         = ~delta_beta3,
  type      = "scatter",
  mode      = "markers",
  marker    = list(
    size        = ~sqrt(n_items) * 2,
    color       = ~rho,
    colorscale  = list(c(0, irw_blue), c(0.5, "#d3d3d3"), c(1, irw_red)),
    cmin        = -1, cmax = 1,
    colorbar    = list(title = "ρ"),
    line        = list(width = 0.5, color = "white")
  ),
  text      = ~hover_text,
  hoverinfo = "text"
) |>
layout(
  xaxis = list(title = "σ_b(treat) / σ_b(ctrl)",
               zeroline = FALSE,
               zerolinecolor = "#aaa",
               showline = TRUE),
  yaxis = list(title = "β₃(M_B) − β₃(M_C)",
               zeroline = TRUE, zerolinecolor = "#aaa", zerolinewidth = 1),
  shapes = list(
    list(type = "line", x0 = 1, x1 = 1,
         y0 = ~min(delta_beta3, na.rm=TRUE), y1 = ~max(delta_beta3, na.rm=TRUE),
         line = list(dash = "dash", color = "#aaa"))
  )
)








Figure 2: Difference in treatment-by-covariate interaction estimates between M_B (constant item effects) and M_C (with IL-HTE), as a function of the ratio of item-difficulty SDs in treatment vs. control groups. Hover over a point for dataset details.




Datasets to the right of the vertical reference line (ratio > 1) tend to show negative \(\hat\beta_3(M_B) - \hat\beta_3(M_C)\): the conventional model produces a more negative interaction estimate than the flexible model, consistent with the theoretical predictions of Gilbert, Miratrix, et al. (2025). This pattern arises because the correlation between item easiness and item-specific treatment effects (\(\rho\)) creates the appearance of heterogeneity by pretest score in a sum-score analysis, even if none exists at the person level.

title: Item-Level Heterogeneous Treatment Effects
text:
Limitations
Dichotomous items only. Items are restricted to those with exactly two response categories; polytomous RCT outcome instruments either lose those items or, if fewer than three dichotomous items remain, are dropped from the analysis entirely. IL-HTE in polytomous outcomes is not examined here.
Only the first wave is used. For datasets with multiple follow-up waves, we use wave 1 only — this vignette doesn’t examine whether item-level treatment effects change over time or across follow-up assessments.
The pretest covariate is chosen from the data. Where a dataset has more than one cov_-prefixed candidate, we pick whichever is most correlated with the response in the control arm — a data-driven choice made before fitting M_B and M_C, rather than a pre-registered or theory-driven selection. This could inflate the apparent size of the M_B/M_C divergence relative to a design that fixed the covariate in advance.
Large datasets are downsampled to at most 5,000 respondent IDs, so results for the largest RCTs in this collection are based on a random subset rather than the full sample.

title: Latent Space Item Response Models: Seeing Local Dependence as Geometry
text:
Note



This vignette – including the dataset search, the compute script, the analysis design, and the writing below – was produced largely by Claude (Anthropic), working from a task specification and with human review. Treat the methodological choices and interpretations accordingly, and check the compute script (lsirm_interaction_maps_compute.R) directly if you’re relying on the numbers here.

title: Latent Space Item Response Models: Seeing Local Dependence as Geometry
text:
Motivation
The Latent Space Item Response Model [LSIRM; Jeon et al. (2021)] adds a single extra term to the Rasch model: a distance penalty between each respondent and each item in a shared, unobserved 2D space, which lets the data decide whether local independence – the assumption that once you condition on a respondent’s position on the latent trait, their responses to different items are unrelated – actually holds. The local dependence vignette checks the same assumption a different way, with Yen’s Q3: fit the model, subtract what it predicts, and see whether anything is left to correlate between item pairs. That residual approach answers “is independence violated” with a number per pair, but it doesn’t show why items and respondents interact, or which respondents are involved. LSIRM’s distance term does both at once: when it isn’t needed, the model collapses back to an ordinary Rasch fit; when it is, respondents and items that share unexplained structure are pulled close together in the space, and the result is directly visualizable: an interaction map. Local dependence stops being an abstract residual correlation and becomes a picture – clusters you can point at.

title: Latent Space Item Response Models: Seeing Local Dependence as Geometry
text:
Method in brief
For a respondent \(j\) and item \(i\) with an ordinary Rasch model, the log-odds of a correct/endorsed response would be \(\theta_j - \beta_i\) (respondent ability minus item difficulty). LSIRM adds one term:
\[\text{logit}\, P(Y_{ji} = 1) = \theta_j + \beta_i - \gamma \lVert z_j - w_i \rVert\]
where \(z_j\) and \(w_i\) are the respondent’s and item’s positions in a shared 2D Euclidean space, and \(\gamma \geq 0\) scales how much that distance matters. When \(\gamma = 0\), the distance term vanishes and the model is the Rasch model; the further \(z_j\) sits from \(w_i\), the more the distance term drags the predicted log-odds down relative to what \(\theta_j -
\beta_i\) alone would predict – interaction the main effects didn’t capture. Fitting the positions and \(\gamma\) jointly by MCMC produces the interaction map: a scatter of item points and respondent points in the same space, where proximity signals shared unexplained structure (a testlet, a common stimulus, a shared response tendency) rather than an ordinary ability/difficulty relationship.
Because \(\gamma = 0\) is a single point on the boundary of \(\gamma \geq 0\), it can’t be tested with an ordinary credible interval the way a normal parameter could. The package used here [lsirm12pl; Go et al. (2025)] implements the spike-and-slab model-selection extension from the original paper (Ishwaran and Rao 2005): a mixture prior on \(\log \gamma\) with a “spike” component concentrated near \(\gamma = 0\) and a “slab” component allowing \(\gamma > 0\), plus an indicator \(\phi\) for which component is active at each MCMC iteration. The posterior mean of \(\phi\) – reported below as the inclusion probability – is the model-selection answer: values near 0 mean the data are consistent with an ordinary Rasch fit; values near 1 mean the interaction term is doing real work. This resolves an open question going into this vignette (see Limitations) – the current CRAN version of lsirm12pl (2.0.3, not the 1.3.9 assumed when this vignette was scoped) exposes spike-and-slab fitting directly via lsirm1pl_ss() (dichotomous items) and lsirmgrm_ss() (graded/polytomous items), so no hand-rolled WAIC comparison was needed.
The graded-response variant is not merely a software convenience. The latent space graded response model has its own development and evaluation (De Carolis et al. 2026), which extends the binary LSIRM of Jeon et al. (2021) to ordered-category responses and is aimed squarely at the Likert-scale self-report instruments that make up most of the study set below. That matters for how the results here should be read: the polytomous fits are an application of a model developed and studied for exactly this kind of data, not an off-label use of a binary method.

title: Latent Space Item Response Models: Seeing Local Dependence as Geometry
text:
Data and methods

Study-set selection
MCMC here is far more expensive per table than the mirt-based models used elsewhere on this site – the original paper’s own examples ran 30-60 minutes per table at N~200-700, I~7-24 – so this vignette deliberately selects 16 tables rather than batch-fitting across all of IRW, in two rounds:
Round 1 (hypothesis-driven, 5 tables), chosen to bracket the diagnostic:


Code
# 1. Tables with known item_family (testlet) structure -- ground truth on
#    which items *should* cluster if LSIRM is picking up real dependence.
#    Cross-referencing the local-dependence vignette's own item_family
#    census: only 2 of ~800 IRW tables carry a usable grouping at all.
#    g308_sirt is dichotomous; chakraborty2026_IWAH_IRW is graded.

# 2. Tables suspected of speededness -- candidates for the "respondents
#    cluster near the last items" pattern described in the LSIRM paper's
#    discussion section. Cross-referenced against the (unmerged)
#    speededness-vignette branch's own classification:
#    credentialform_lnirt and nature_relatedness were both flagged
#    "likely speeded" there.

# 3. A presumed-Rasch-like negative control with no known family/testlet
#    structure and no speededness suspicion: blum_2018_imak_bin.


Round 2 (expansion, 11 more tables), added after Round 1 cleared the go/no-go bar and raised a “what predicts a positive finding” question that needed more data points:


Code
# 4. The remaining 5 tables classified "likely speeded" by the same
#    speededness screen, completing that bucket in full: brain_hemisphere,
#    artistic_preferences, depression_anxiety_stress, fisher_temperment,
#    face_memory_test.

# 5. A *blind* random sample (seed 20260723) of 6 more tables from
#    irw_filter(n_items = c(5, 60), n_participants = c(100, 5000)),
#    excluding every table already in the study set -- deliberately not
#    hand-picked for any hypothesis: sd3ypl_klimczak_2019_ses,
#    BPAQ_Christopher_2024_PSS10, prpt_hellmann_2021_conscientiousness,
#    chen2026_sc, disgust_berger2014, autism_blotner_2025_s1_aq.

Per-table computation
For each table, fit_lsirm() in the compute script:

Fetches the wide response matrix directly via irw_fetch(table, resp = TRUE), and separately fetches the long format to recover item_family (if present) and a within-person item-presentation-order column (same fallback logic as the speededness vignette: a named order column if one exists, first-appearance order otherwise).
Downsamples respondents to at most 700 and items to at most 40, mirroring the downsampling pattern already used in 2PL across datasets. Item downsampling always keeps the true last 10 items by presentation order (so the “stragglers near the end” check below stays meaningful) and systematically samples the rest; this triggered for every table with more than 40 items (credentialform_lnirt, depression_anxiety_stress, fisher_temperment, face_memory_test, artistic_preferences).
Fits the 1PL LSIRM with spike-and-slab (lsirm1pl_ss()) for dichotomous tables, or the graded-response variant [lsirmgrm_ss(); De Carolis et al. (2026)] for polytomous tables, both with a 2D latent space and the full 15,000-iteration MCMC settings (2,500 burn-in, thinned by 5), matching the original paper’s defaults.
Records posterior mean item and respondent positions, the \(\gamma\) posterior mean and 95% credible interval, the inclusion probability, and BIC.



Code
fit_lsirm <- function(table_name) {
  mat <- fetch_wide(table_name)  # irw_fetch(resp = TRUE), cleaned, downsampled
  fit <- if (is_dichotomous) lsirm1pl_ss(mat, ndim = 2) else lsirmgrm_ss(mat, ndim = 2)
  # gamma_estimate, pi_estimate (inclusion probability), z_estimate, w_estimate ...
}








Note



To reproduce with current IRW holdings, re-run lsirm_interaction_maps_compute.R --full and commit the updated lsirmdata/lsirm_interaction_maps_results_full.rds.

In plain terms: “inclusion probability” is the model’s own confidence, on a 0-to-1 scale, that the extra “interaction” ingredient is actually needed to explain the data – above 0.5 means “yes, include it”; near 1 means “yes, almost certainly”; near 0 means “no, an ordinary Rasch model already explains this fine.” Read that way, the table above says something striking: every single one of the 13 multi-point-scale tables – including all 6 that were picked completely at random, with no reason to expect anything special – comes back with the model over 96% sure the interaction ingredient is needed. The 3 right/wrong tables split the way we originally expected going in: two come back near-certain it’s not needed (g308_sirt, blum_2018_imak_bin), and one comes back the most certain of anything in the whole set that it is needed (credentialform_lnirt, at 99.96% confidence). A split that tracks question format (right/wrong vs. multi-point scale) this cleanly – especially once random, unrelated tables were thrown in and still followed the same pattern – is a red flag worth checking before trusting it as a real finding about these tables, rather than a quirk of how the tool handles multi-point scales. That check is the next section.


Interaction maps


Code
build_position_df <- function(tbl) {
  pos <- positions[[tbl]]
  z <- as.data.frame(pos$z); names(z)[1:2] <- c("dim1", "dim2")
  z$type <- "respondent"; z$label <- rownames(pos$z); z$family <- NA_character_
  w <- as.data.frame(pos$w); names(w)[1:2] <- c("dim1", "dim2")
  w$type <- "item"; w$label <- rownames(pos$w)
  fam <- item_family_list[[tbl]]
  w$family <- if (!is.null(fam)) as.character(fam$item_family[match(w$label, fam$item)]) else NA_character_
  df <- bind_rows(z[, c("dim1","dim2","type","label","family")],
                  w[, c("dim1","dim2","type","label","family")])
  df$table <- tbl
  df
}

position_df <- bind_rows(lapply(summary_df$table, build_position_df))

panel_order <- summary_df |> arrange(is_dichotomous, desc(pi_estimate)) |> pull(table)
panel_labels <- setNames(
  sprintf("%s (P[gamma>0] = %.2f)", summary_df$table, summary_df$pi_estimate),
  summary_df$table
)
position_df$panel <- factor(panel_labels[position_df$table], levels = panel_labels[panel_order])

ggplot(position_df, aes(x = dim1, y = dim2, shape = type)) +
  geom_point(data = filter(position_df, is.na(family)), colour = irw_grey, alpha = 0.5, size = 1.4) +
  geom_point(data = filter(position_df, !is.na(family)), aes(colour = family), size = 2.2) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(respondent = 16, item = 17)) +
  facet_wrap(~panel, scales = "free", ncol = 4) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, shape = NULL, colour = "item_family") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", strip.text = element_text(size = 8))








Figure 1: Interaction maps for all 16 study-set tables, grouped by response format (dichotomous first) and sorted by posterior inclusion probability within format. Points are posterior mean positions in the shared 2D latent space: circles are respondents, triangles are items. Items sharing a known item_family grouping (where available) are colored; all other points are grey. Panel titles show each table’s posterior inclusion probability for gamma > 0.





chakraborty2026_IWAH_IRW (top group, colored by item_family) shows visibly tighter item clustering by group than the two near-null dichotomous panels’ diffuse scatter. Beyond that one labeled case, though, the maps mostly demonstrate the same thing the gamma table does: broad, structured spread across nearly every polytomous panel regardless of role (speededness suspect or blind exploratory), and near-patternless noise in g308_sirt and blum_2018_imak_bin.

title: Latent Space Item Response Models: Seeing Local Dependence as Geometry
section: Is this really about response format, or is the estimator biased?
text:
Is this really about response format, or is the estimator biased?
A split this clean – every multi-point-scale table positive, most right/wrong tables null – is more consistent with a quirk in the tool than with 13 independent real discoveries. Put plainly: before believing “multi-point scales have hidden structure and right/wrong tests mostly don’t,” we need to rule out the boring explanation that the fitting method itself just runs hot on any multi-point-scale data, whether or not anything real is going on. So the question gets turned on the tool: does lsirmgrm_ss() (the multi-point-scale version of the fitting method) claim high confidence on any multi-point-scale data, even data we build by hand to have zero true interaction?


Code
# Simulate a clean single-factor GRM dataset: realistic item discrimination
# and category thresholds, N/I matched to the study set, gamma = 0 by
# construction (no interaction structure of any kind).
a <- matrix(rlnorm(20, 0, 0.3), ncol = 1)
d <- matrix(t(apply(matrix(rnorm(20 * 4), ncol = 4), 1, function(x) sort(x, decreasing = TRUE))), ncol = 4)
sim_dat <- mirt::simdata(a, d, N = 700, itemtype = "graded")
sim_fit <- lsirmgrm_ss(sim_dat, ndim = 2, niter = 15000, nburn = 2500, nthin = 5)




Code
tibble(
  case             = c("Simulated null GRM data (this check)", "Real polytomous tables (range, n=13)"),
  pi_estimate      = c(.cache$null_calibration$pi_estimate,
                       paste0(sprintf("%.3f", min(summary_df$pi_estimate[!summary_df$is_dichotomous])),
                              " to ",
                              sprintf("%.3f", max(summary_df$pi_estimate[!summary_df$is_dichotomous])))),
  gamma            = c(sprintf("%.3f", .cache$null_calibration$gamma_mean),
                       paste0(sprintf("%.2f", min(summary_df$gamma_mean[!summary_df$is_dichotomous])),
                              " to ",
                              sprintf("%.2f", max(summary_df$gamma_mean[!summary_df$is_dichotomous]))))
) |>
  knitr::kable(col.names = c("Case", "P(gamma > 0)", "Gamma"))
